items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: My Grammys are notes for — I think for Art Tatum, for Louis Armstrong, for Fats Waller, for Erroll Garner, for Clifford Brown.

ctx.x: No kidding. And of the Grammys you received, would you have said yes, that was some of my best work?

Well, as I usually would say when I got these Grammys, it’s no great — it’s due to the great musicians that I was able to write about and the great music that I was able to write about. My Grammys are notes for — I think for Art Tatum, for Louis Armstrong, for Fats Waller, for Erroll Garner, for Clifford Brown. Hey. You know.

Right. That’s a heck of a good start. I wanted to ask you about — I guess this would be sort of a current question. I’ve had some conversations recently with a professor about women in jazz. And I wonder if you have any thoughts about the question of why isn’t there more?

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We did Erroll Garner, which was difficult because of – I like Martha Glaser very much, but she is a demanding person. But she wasn’t there. Erroll was a dream to work with.

ctx.x: What happened was after I left Down Beat, I fortunately had established enough of a reputation so that I managed, because I had married again. 1975, which was the year after I left Down Beat, my first child was born. My son Adam was born in September 1975. So I did have a family to support. I had gotten a contract to write a book with the Danish photographer Ole Brask. It was Ole’s then girlfriend, who was then involved in the publishing business, who got this contact for us. So he was – what I should say, he was…

We did do a series. The series came out pretty well. Dexter Gordon was visiting. So we did him. Don Byas was visiting. So we managed to do him. We did Bobby Hackett and Vic Dickenson with Don DeMicheal on drums. I got Don on the show. We did Erroll Garner, which was difficult because of – I like Martha Glaser very much, but she is a demanding person. But she wasn’t there. Erroll was a dream to work with. A wonderful show. How did I get into this? Because I was saying something about television.
You were talking about traveling around and Jazz People, the book.
